nodes.title: Dockerfile: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Dockerfile. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Which Dockerfile instruction sets the default command that runs when a container?
flashcards.back: CMD sets the default command and/or arguments for a container. It can be completely overridden by providing a command at `docker run`. ENTRYPOINT sets the main executable and is harder to override (requires --entrypoint flag). RUN executes commands during image build. EXEC is not a Dockerfile instruction.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a `.dockerignore` file?
flashcards.back: The .dockerignore file works like .gitignore — it tells the Docker CLI which files and directories to exclude when sending the build context to the daemon. This speeds up builds (smaller context), prevents accidentally including secrets (e.g., .env, credentials), and avoids cache-busting from unrelated file changes.

flashcards.front: What is a multi-stage Dockerfile build and what is its primary benefit?
flashcards.back: Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM instructions. Build stages compile/test code with all required build tools. The final stage copies only the compiled artifacts, resulting in a minimal image without compilers, test frameworks, or intermediate files. For example, a Go app: stage 1 uses golang:alpine to compile, stage 2 uses scratch or alpine and copies just the binary — reducing image size from GB to MB. producing a smaller final image without build tools

flashcards.front: What is the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?
flashcards.back: COPY simply copies files/directories from the build context into the image. ADD additionally: (1) can fetch files from remote URLs, (2) automatically extracts local tar archives (.tar, .tar.gz, etc.) into the destination. Best practice: use COPY by default. Use ADD only when you specifically need URL fetching or tar extraction — its implicit behavior can cause unexpected results. COPY only copies local files/directories — COPY is preferred when you don't need ADD's extra features

nodes.title: Swarm: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Swarm. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Which command creates a Docker Swarm and makes the current node a manager?
flashcards.back: `docker swarm init` initializes a new Swarm and promotes the current node to manager. On machines with multiple network interfaces, add `--advertise-addr IP` to specify the manager's address for other nodes to join. After init, Docker outputs a `docker swarm join --token` command for adding worker nodes.

flashcards.front: In Docker Swarm, what is the difference between a service and a task?
flashcards.back: A Swarm service declares desired state: which image to run, how many replicas, resource limits, placement constraints, update policies, etc. The Swarm manager decomposes the service into tasks — each task maps to exactly one container on one node. If a task fails, the manager creates a replacement task to maintain desired replica count. replicas, ports, constraints); a task is the atomic unit of scheduling — one container instance running the service on a specific node

flashcards.front: How do you scale a running Swarm service named 'webapp' to 5 replicas?
flashcards.back: `docker service scale webapp=5` sets the replica count for the 'webapp' service to 5. You can scale multiple services at once: `docker service scale webapp=5 api=3`. Alternatively: `docker service update --replicas=5 webapp`. The Swarm manager will schedule new tasks on available nodes or terminate tasks if scaling down.

flashcards.front: A Swarm service update is in progress and several tasks have become unhealthy. W?
flashcards.back: `--update-failure-action=pause` stops the rolling update when a task fails, allowing operators to investigate. Other values: `continue` (default: keep updating even if tasks fail), `rollback` (automatically revert to the previous service spec). Combine with `--update-monitor` (time to observe a task before considering it healthy) and `--update-max-failure-ratio`.

nodes.title: Security: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Security. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is Docker Content Trust (DCT) and what does it protect against?
flashcards.back: Docker Content Trust (DCT) uses The Update Framework (TUF) and Notary to sign and verify images. When enabled (DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1), Docker only pulls/runs images with valid signatures. It protects against: man-in-the-middle attacks substituting a legitimate image, running unverified third-party images, and supply chain tampering. Signers use offline root keys and online targets keys.

flashcards.front: What Linux kernel feature does Docker use to limit a container's CPU and memory ?
flashcards.back: Control groups (cgroups) enforce resource limits: CPU shares, CPU quotas, memory limits, block I/O, network bandwidth. For example: `docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 myimage`. Linux namespaces provide isolation (PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user namespaces). seccomp limits available syscalls. AppArmor/SELinux enforce MAC policies. Together, these form Docker's container isolation model.

flashcards.front: What is the recommended way to pass secrets (passwords, API keys) to containers ?
flashcards.back: Docker Secrets (Swarm only) stores sensitive data encrypted in the Swarm's Raft log. Secrets are decrypted and mounted as in-memory tmpfs files at /run/secrets/SECRET_NAME inside authorized containers — never written to disk. Environment variables are visible in `docker inspect` output and process listings. Hardcoding in images is an obvious anti-pattern. `docker secret create` and `docker service create --secret`.

flashcards.front: What does the `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` combination achieve wh?
flashcards.back: Linux capabilities break root privileges into distinct units. `--cap-drop ALL` removes all capabilities from the container. `--cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` re-adds only the capability to bind to privileged ports (<1024). This follows the principle of least privilege — the container can run a web server on port 80 without any other elevated privileges. Never add SYS_ADMIN unless absolutely necessary. following the principle of least privilege

nodes.title: Networking: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Networking. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What network driver creates an isolated network for containers on a single host ?
flashcards.back: The bridge driver (default for single-host) creates an isolated virtual network. Containers get private IPs and can communicate within the bridge network. Docker performs NAT so containers can reach the internet via the host. The host driver removes network isolation (container shares host's network stack). The overlay driver is for multi-host Swarm networking. none disables networking.

flashcards.front: Containers on the same custom bridge network communicate using container names. ?
flashcards.back: User-defined bridge networks include an embedded DNS server that resolves container names to their IPs. The default bridge network (docker0) does not have this — containers must use --link (deprecated) or IP addresses to communicate. This is a key reason to always create custom networks: automatic service discovery by name, better isolation, and network-level container grouping.

flashcards.front: What does the overlay network driver provide in Docker Swarm?
flashcards.back: Overlay networks span multiple Docker hosts (Swarm nodes), enabling containers on different physical/virtual machines to communicate using private IPs. Docker encapsulates traffic in VXLAN packets for host-to-host transport. Overlay networks are the foundation of Swarm service discovery and load balancing. They can be encrypted with --opt encrypted for node-to-node TLS.

flashcards.front: A container must NOT have network access. Which network driver should you use?
flashcards.back: The 'none' network driver completely disables networking for the container. The container has only a loopback interface. Use it for containers processing local data with no network requirements (batch jobs, file processing), security-sensitive workloads, or containers that should not communicate with anything. `docker run --network=none myimage`.

nodes.title: Mixed Topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Mixed Topics. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A container needs to persist data that survives container removal. Which storage?
flashcards.back: Named Docker volumes are managed by Docker, portable, easy to back up, and work across different host paths. Bind mounts couple the container to a specific host path, reducing portability. tmpfs mounts are in-memory and lost when the container stops. The container's writable layer is removed with the container. Named volumes are the recommended production storage solution.

flashcards.front: Which command lists all volumes on a Docker host, including their names and driv?
flashcards.back: `docker volume ls` lists all volumes with their driver and name. To filter: `docker volume ls -f dangling=true` shows volumes not mounted by any container. To remove unused volumes: `docker volume prune`. To inspect a specific volume (including mount point): `docker volume inspect VOLUME_NAME`.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a bind mount and a Docker volume?
flashcards.back: Bind mounts: `docker run -v /host/path:/container/path` — tightly couples the container to a specific host directory. Great for development (live code editing) but reduces portability. Docker volumes: `docker run -v myvolume:/container/path` — Docker manages the storage location (/var/lib/docker/volumes/), independent lifecycle, easier to backup/migrate, work with volume drivers for cloud storage (EBS, NFS, etc.). Docker volumes are managed by Docker with their own lifecycle independent of containers

flashcards.front: What is a tmpfs mount in Docker and when is it appropriate?
flashcards.back: tmpfs mounts are stored in the host's memory only (never on disk). Data is temporary — lost when the container stops or restarts. Use cases: storing session tokens, credentials, or other sensitive data that should never touch disk; high-performance temporary scratch space. `docker run --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m myimage`. Available only on Linux. For secrets: use Docker Secrets in Swarm instead. data is never written to disk and is lost when the container stops; ideal for sensitive temporary data
